summary: Nervous system tumors are sorted on the exam by age, location, and histology. Children get mostly posterior fossa tumors (medulloblastoma, pilocytic astrocytoma) and neuroblastoma outside the brain; adults get metastases, glioblastoma, and meningioma. Know the classic slide for each tumor and the genetic syndromes (NF1, NF2, tuberous sclerosis, von Hippel-Lindau) that cause them.

points: Adults: most intracranial tumors are metastases; the most common primary tumor is meningioma; the most common primary malignant tumor is glioblastoma.

Meningioma: dural-based, extra-axial tumor of arachnoid cap cells, most often in adult women; whorls and psammoma bodies; linked to NF2 and prior radiation; causes seizures or focal deficits by compression.
Adult primary tumors are mostly supratentorial; childhood brain tumors are mostly infratentorial (posterior fossa).
Brain metastases come mainly from lung, breast, melanoma, kidney, and colon; they are often multiple and sit at the gray-white junction.
Primary CNS lymphoma is a diffuse large B cell lymphoma; in AIDS it is EBV-driven and can look like a ring-enhancing mass, mimicking toxoplasmosis.
notes.why: Metastases outnumber primary tumors because the brain receives about 15 to 20 percent of cardiac output, and tumor emboli lodge where arterioles narrow at the gray-white junction. Meningioma grows from arachnoid cap cells outside the brain parenchyma, so it compresses tissue instead of infiltrating it, and its symptoms come from mass effect. Loss of merlin (NF2) and radiation-induced DNA damage both remove growth control in meningothelial cells. In AIDS, loss of T cell surveillance lets EBV-transformed B cells expand, which explains primary CNS lymphoma.

points: Glioblastoma: IDH-wildtype astrocytic tumor of older adults, grade 4, GFAP positive.
Glioblastoma spreads along white matter and can cross the corpus callosum (butterfly glioma).
Glioblastoma slide: pseudopalisading tumor cells around necrosis plus microvascular proliferation; median survival is only about 15 months with treatment.
Diffuse astrocytoma in younger adults is usually IDH-mutant and grows slowly but can progress to a higher grade.
Oligodendroglioma: IDH-mutant with 1p/19q codeletion, frontal lobe, calcified, presents with seizures; fried-egg cells and chicken-wire capillaries.
Pilocytic astrocytoma: child, cerebellum, cyst with a mural nodule, Rosenthal fibers, BRAF alteration, grade 1 with a good prognosis after resection.
notes.why: Gliomas are now defined by molecular markers. Mutant IDH makes the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate, which inhibits DNA and histone demethylases and marks the slower astrocytoma and oligodendroglioma lineage; glioblastoma is IDH-wildtype and outgrows its blood supply. Hypoxic necrosis induces VEGF through HIF-1 alpha, which explains the microvascular proliferation and the ring of enhancement on imaging. Tumor cells migrate along white matter tracts, including the corpus callosum, so surgery cannot remove every cell and recurrence is expected.

points: Medulloblastoma: most common malignant brain tumor of childhood, arises in the cerebellum (usually the vermis).
Small round blue cells with Homer Wright rosettes; it is highly malignant but radiosensitive.
It can compress the fourth ventricle (obstructive hydrocephalus, truncal ataxia) and seed the CSF as drop metastases to the spinal cord.
Ganglioglioma: mixed neoplastic ganglion cells and glial cells, temporal lobe, children and young adults, chronic seizures, slow growth.
Central neurocytoma: uniform round neuronal cells inside the lateral ventricle near the foramen of Monro in young adults; can block CSF flow.
notes.why: Medulloblastoma is an embryonal tumor built from undifferentiated precursor cells (one subgroup arises from cerebellar granule cell precursors), which is why it looks like sheets of small round blue cells. A vermis mass sits directly on the fourth ventricle, so it blocks CSF outflow and raises intracranial pressure, while vermis damage itself causes truncal ataxia. Cells shed into the CSF settle on the spinal cord and cauda equina, so staging images the whole neuraxis. Ganglioglioma causes epilepsy by irritating the temporal cortex, and central neurocytoma causes symptoms by blocking the foramen of Monro.

points: Neural crest tumor of young children (most under age 5); the adrenal medulla is the most common site, but it can arise anywhere along the sympathetic chain.
Presents as an abdominal mass that can cross the midline; urinary HVA and VMA (catecholamine breakdown products) are high.
Homer Wright rosettes; stains for neuron-specific markers such as synaptophysin.
Opsoclonus-myoclonus (dancing eyes, dancing feet) is a paraneoplastic sign.
MYCN amplification predicts aggressive disease; some infant tumors regress on their own.
notes.why: Neuroblastoma comes from neural crest cells that would normally become sympathetic neurons and adrenal chromaffin cells, so it can arise anywhere along the sympathetic chain and it makes catecholamines. MAO and COMT break dopamine down to HVA and norepinephrine and epinephrine down to VMA, which is why these metabolites rise in the urine. Retroperitoneal tumors grow around vessels and often cross the midline, unlike Wilms tumor, which stays within the kidney. MYCN amplification drives proliferation and predicts poor outcome, and opsoclonus-myoclonus reflects an immune response against tumor antigens that also targets neurons.

points: Schwannoma: S-100 positive Schwann cells; cellular Antoni A areas with Verocay bodies (palisaded nuclei) and loose Antoni B areas.
Vestibular schwannoma at the cerebellopontine angle: unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, imbalance; large tumors compress CN V and VII.
NF2 (merlin gene, chromosome 22): bilateral vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, ependymomas.
NF1 (neurofibromin gene, chromosome 17): neurofibromin normally turns off Ras, so its loss drives Ras signaling.
NF1 findings: café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, cutaneous neurofibromas, Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas), optic pathway glioma, pheochromocytoma.
Plexiform neurofibromas in NF1 can turn into malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor.
notes.why: Schwannoma is a clonal proliferation of Schwann cells that grows beside the nerve and pushes axons aside, while a neurofibroma mixes Schwann cells, fibroblasts, and axons running through it. A vestibular schwannoma begins in the internal auditory canal and expands into the cerebellopontine angle, so hearing loss and tinnitus come first and CN V and VII signs come later. NF1 and NF2 are autosomal dominant tumor suppressor disorders: a tumor forms when a cell carrying the inherited mutation loses the second allele. Neurofibromin is a Ras GTPase-activating protein, so its loss keeps Ras GTP-bound and drives MAPK growth signaling.

notes.h: Eye tumors and other tumor syndromes
points: Retinoblastoma: leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) in a young child; RB1 on chromosome 13 needs two hits.
Hereditary retinoblastoma (germline first hit) is often bilateral and carries a later risk of osteosarcoma.
Uveal melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults and spreads by blood, often to the liver.
Tuberous sclerosis (TSC1 or TSC2, overactive mTOR): cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, seizures, ash-leaf spots, cardiac rhabdomyoma, renal angiomyolipoma.
von Hippel-Lindau (VHL on chromosome 3, HIF not degraded): cerebellar and retinal hemangioblastomas, clear cell renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytoma.
notes.why: RB protein holds E2F inactive and blocks the G1 to S transition, so a retinal cell becomes malignant only after both RB1 alleles are lost (Knudson two-hit model). A child who inherits one mutant allele needs only one somatic hit per cell, which explains earlier onset, bilateral tumors, and later sarcomas in other tissues. TSC1 and TSC2 normally restrain mTOR, and the VHL protein normally tags HIF for degradation, so loss of VHL produces constant HIF-driven VEGF that explains the highly vascular hemangioblastomas and clear cell renal carcinomas. Uveal melanoma spreads by blood because the inside of the eye has no lymphatic drainage.

flows.title: Medulloblastoma: from vermis mass to raised pressure
steps: Embryonal tumor grows in the cerebellar vermis of a child.
The mass compresses the fourth ventricle and blocks CSF outflow.
Lateral and third ventricles dilate (obstructive hydrocephalus).
Intracranial pressure rises: morning headache, vomiting, papilledema.

flows.title: Glioblastoma: necrosis to new vessels
steps: Rapid tumor growth outstrips the blood supply.
Central hypoxia causes tumor necrosis.
Hypoxia stabilizes HIF-1 alpha in surviving tumor cells.
HIF-1 alpha raises VEGF production.
VEGF drives microvascular proliferation with leaky vessels.
Leaky vessels cause vasogenic edema and ring enhancement on contrast imaging.

flows.title: NF1: from gene loss to neurofibroma
steps: A germline NF1 mutation on chromosome 17 inactivates one allele.
A Schwann lineage cell loses the second NF1 allele.
Without neurofibromin, a Ras GTPase-activating protein, Ras stays GTP-bound.
Constant Ras signaling through the MAPK cascade drives proliferation.
Neurofibromas form; plexiform ones can become malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors.

tricks.label: Two tumors share Homer Wright rosettes
tricks.text: Medulloblastoma (in the cerebellum) and neuroblastoma (in the adrenal) are both small round blue cell tumors of childhood with Homer Wright rosettes. Location and urine HVA and VMA tell them apart.

tricks.label: NF1 and NF2 by chromosome
tricks.text: NF1 is on chromosome 17 (17 letters in von Recklinghausen), and NF2 is on chromosome 22 (two 2s, two ears, so bilateral acoustic schwannomas).

tricks.label: Child versus adult tumor site
tricks.text: Children's brain tumors sit low (posterior fossa); adults' sit high (cerebral hemispheres). Check the age and the site before you look at the histology.

highYield: Metastases outnumber primary brain tumors in adults; lung is the most common source.
Glioblastoma: pseudopalisading necrosis, can cross the corpus callosum, GFAP positive.
Meningioma: dural-based, whorls and psammoma bodies, women, NF2, prior radiation.
Pilocytic astrocytoma: child, cerebellar cyst with mural nodule, Rosenthal fibers.
Medulloblastoma can spread through CSF and cause drop metastases in the spinal cord.
Neuroblastoma with MYCN amplification has a poor prognosis; watch for opsoclonus-myoclonus.
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas mean NF2.
Hemangioblastoma plus renal cell carcinoma means von Hippel-Lindau.
pitfalls: Meningioma is extra-axial (outside the brain tissue, attached to dura); gliomas are intra-axial and infiltrate the brain.
Psammoma bodies point to meningioma in the CNS; Rosenthal fibers point to pilocytic astrocytoma. Do not swap them.
Neuroblastoma and Wilms tumor both present as abdominal masses in children; neuroblastoma is adrenal, can cross the midline, and raises HVA and VMA.
A ring-enhancing lesion in AIDS can be toxoplasmosis or primary CNS lymphoma; a single lesion with EBV DNA in CSF favors lymphoma.
Oligodendroglioma (fried-egg cells) and central neurocytoma both have round uniform cells; neurocytoma sits inside the lateral ventricle.

summary: CNS and PNS infections are tested by matching the patient (age, immune status, exposure) to the organism and then to the lesion. Know the bacterial meningitis organisms by age, the CSF patterns, the toxin diseases (botulism and tetanus), the slow and opportunistic infections (prions, PML, SSPE, cryptococcus), and how each organism reaches the nervous system.

points: Neonates: group B streptococcus, E. coli, and Listeria.
Children and adults: S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis; older adults add Listeria.
Findings: fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, altered mental status; a petechial or purpuric rash suggests meningococcemia.
Complications: sensorineural hearing loss, hydrocephalus, seizures, cerebral infarction, and adrenal hemorrhage with meningococcemia (Waterhouse-Friderichsen).
Tuberculous meningitis forms a thick basilar exudate that traps cranial nerves (palsies) and blocks CSF flow (hydrocephalus).
Spirochetes: Lyme disease gives lymphocytic meningitis, facial palsy (often bilateral), and radiculopathy; leptospirosis comes from water contaminated by animal urine.
notes.why: The organism list follows age and immunity: neonates acquire group B streptococcus and E. coli from the birth canal, and Listeria, an intracellular organism controlled by cell-mediated immunity, targets newborns and older adults whose T cell defenses are weaker. Encapsulated bacteria colonize the nasopharynx, resist phagocytosis in the blood, and cross into the subarachnoid space, where bacterial products trigger cytokine release and a neutrophil exudate that raises intracranial pressure and injures nearby nerves and vessels. Meningococcal endotoxin triggers disseminated intravascular coagulation, which causes purpura and adrenal hemorrhage. Tuberculous exudate collects at the base of the brain, where it traps exiting cranial nerves and blocks CSF flow.

points: Viral encephalitis histology: perivascular lymphocytic cuffs, microglial nodules, and neuronophagia.
HSV-1: the most common cause of sporadic fatal viral encephalitis; hemorrhagic necrosis of the temporal lobes, with confusion and personality change.
Arboviruses (West Nile, St. Louis, eastern and western equine) cycle between mosquitoes and birds; humans are dead-end hosts. West Nile can cause acute flaccid paralysis in older adults.
Rabies travels retrogradely up peripheral nerves after a bat, raccoon, or dog bite; Negri bodies in neurons, agitation, and hydrophobia from painful pharyngeal spasm.
Brain abscess spreads from a nearby sinus, ear, mastoid, or tooth, or seeds by blood from endocarditis, lung infection, or a right-to-left shunt that bypasses the lung filter.
Abscess organisms: streptococci, staphylococci, and anaerobes; a ring-enhancing lesion with headache, fever, and focal deficits. Lumbar puncture risks herniation.
notes.why: Encephalitis is infection of the brain parenchyma itself, so lymphocytes gather around vessels (perivascular cuffs) and microglia cluster around and engulf dying neurons (neuronophagia). HSV-1 favors the medial temporal and inferior frontal lobes, the limbic regions that handle memory and emotion, which explains confusion, personality change, and seizures. Rabies virus binds the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction and then moves to the CNS by retrograde axonal transport, so the incubation period depends on the distance from bite to brain. An abscess starts as cerebritis and is then walled off by a collagen capsule that forms the enhancing ring, and its mass effect makes lumbar puncture dangerous.

points: Cryptococcus in AIDS (low CD4 count): subacute headache, raised opening pressure, positive cryptococcal capsular antigen, India ink shows the capsule.
Mucormycosis in diabetic ketoacidosis: hyphae invade vessels, causing a black necrotic eschar of the nose or palate that spreads to the orbit and brain.
Toxoplasma gondii in AIDS: multiple ring-enhancing lesions; from cat feces or undercooked meat.
Neurocysticercosis: swallowed Taenia solium eggs (fecal-oral) become brain cysts that cause seizures.
Naegleria fowleri: warm freshwater swimming; the amoeba enters through the cribriform plate and causes rapidly fatal meningoencephalitis.
notes.why: Cryptococcus and Toxoplasma are normally contained by CD4 T cell help to macrophages, so they cause CNS disease once the CD4 count falls, usually below about 100 cells/µL. Cryptococcal capsular polysaccharide builds up in the subarachnoid space and impairs CSF absorption at the arachnoid granulations, which explains the very high opening pressure. Mucor needs iron and thrives in acidic, hyperglycemic tissue; in ketoacidosis, acidosis frees iron from transferrin, and the hyphae invade vessel walls, causing thrombosis and black infarcted tissue. In neurocysticercosis, seizures come mainly from the inflammation around a degenerating cyst.

points: HSV-2: aseptic meningitis in adults and neonatal encephalitis after birth canal exposure.
CMV: encephalitis and retinitis in advanced AIDS; congenital CMV gives periventricular calcifications and hearing loss.
EBV: primary CNS lymphoma in AIDS.
VZV stays latent in dorsal root and cranial nerve ganglia and reactivates as painful dermatomal shingles.
Zoster ophthalmicus involves V1 and can damage the eye; Ramsay Hunt syndrome (geniculate ganglion) gives facial palsy with vesicles in the ear.
Postherpetic neuralgia is pain that persists after the rash heals, more common in older adults.
notes.why: All herpesviruses establish lifelong latency, so CNS disease often comes from reactivation when cell-mediated immunity falls with age or immune suppression. VZV hides in sensory ganglia after chickenpox and, when it reactivates, travels down the sensory axon to the skin, which is why the rash follows a single dermatome and pain often comes before the vesicles. The ganglion involved predicts the syndrome: V1 reactivation threatens the cornea, and geniculate ganglion reactivation paralyzes the face and puts vesicles in the ear. Inflammatory damage to the ganglion and nerve leaves abnormal pain signaling that persists as postherpetic neuralgia.

points: Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release: descending symmetric flaccid paralysis starting with cranial nerves, with no fever and no sensory loss.
Foodborne botulism comes from preformed toxin; infant botulism from swallowed spores (honey) that make toxin in the gut; wound botulism from spores growing in a wound.
Tetanus toxin travels to the spinal cord and blocks GABA and glycine release from inhibitory interneurons: trismus, risus sardonicus, opisthotonus, spastic paralysis.
Polio: fecal-oral enterovirus that destroys anterior horn cells, causing asymmetric flaccid paralysis with areflexia and normal sensation.
Prion disease: normal alpha-helical PrP refolds into protease-resistant beta-pleated PrP; rapid dementia, myoclonus, spongiform change with no inflammation.
PML: JC virus reactivates in severe immunosuppression and destroys oligodendrocytes, causing multifocal white matter demyelination.
SSPE: defective measles virus persists after early childhood measles and appears years later as cognitive decline and myoclonus.
notes.why: Botulinum and tetanus toxins are both zinc proteases that cleave SNARE proteins and block vesicle release, and the synapse they reach decides the picture. Botulinum toxin stays at the peripheral cholinergic terminal, causing flaccid paralysis, while tetanus toxin travels retrogradely to the spinal cord and silences inhibitory interneurons, so motor neurons fire unopposed and muscles become rigid. Poliovirus kills lower motor neurons in the anterior horn, so paralysis is flaccid and areflexic while sensory pathways are spared. Misfolded PrP converts normal PrP into more protease-resistant beta-sheet protein that accumulates and kills neurons, leaving vacuoles with no immune response.

points: M. leprae prefers cool body sites and invades Schwann cells of peripheral nerves.
Tuberculoid leprosy: strong Th1 response, few bacilli, a few anesthetic hypopigmented plaques, thickened nerves.
Lepromatous leprosy: Th2 response, many bacilli, leonine facies, symmetric glove-and-stocking neuropathy.
Tertiary neurosyphilis: meningovascular disease (strokes), general paresis (dementia, personality change), and tabes dorsalis.
Tabes dorsalis destroys dorsal roots and dorsal columns: sensory ataxia, positive Romberg sign, Argyll Robertson pupils, Charcot joints. A positive CSF VDRL confirms neurosyphilis.
notes.why: The form of leprosy depends on the host T cell response: a Th1 response (IFN-gamma activating macrophages) builds granulomas that contain the bacilli but damage nearby nerves, while a Th2 response fails to activate macrophages, so bacilli multiply and spread widely. M. leprae grows best below core body temperature, which is why it favors the skin, nose, and superficial nerves. In tabes dorsalis, inflammation destroys the dorsal roots and the dorsal columns degenerate, so proprioception is lost, causing sensory ataxia and a positive Romberg sign. Loss of joint position and pain sense leads to repeated unnoticed injury and joint destruction (Charcot joints).

flows.title: Bacterial meningitis pathogenesis
steps: Encapsulated bacteria colonize the nasopharynx.
They invade the blood, where the capsule resists phagocytosis.
Bacteria cross the blood-brain or blood-CSF barrier into the subarachnoid space.
Bacterial products trigger cytokine release (IL-1, TNF) and neutrophil influx.
Barrier breakdown and inflammation cause cerebral edema and raised intracranial pressure.
Falling cerebral perfusion, vasculitis, and infarction cause neurologic damage.

flows.title: Tetanus: wound to spastic paralysis
steps: C. tetani spores enter a contaminated puncture wound.
In anaerobic tissue, spores germinate and release tetanospasmin.
Toxin enters motor nerve terminals and travels retrogradely to the spinal cord.
Toxin passes into inhibitory interneurons and cleaves synaptobrevin.
GABA and glycine release stops, so motor neurons fire unopposed.
Sustained contraction: trismus, risus sardonicus, opisthotonus.

flows.title: Prion disease
steps: Misfolded PrP arises sporadically, from a PRNP mutation, or by exposure.
Misfolded PrP binds normal alpha-helical PrP.
It templates the normal protein into beta-pleated, protease-resistant PrP.
Aggregates accumulate and neurons die.
Vacuoles form (spongiform change) with no inflammation.
Rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus follows.

tricks.label: Botulism goes down, tetanus locks up
tricks.text: Botulism blocks acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, so muscles go limp from the head downward. Tetanus blocks the inhibitory neurons in the cord, so muscles stay contracted.

tricks.label: Tuberculoid tight, lepromatous loose
tricks.text: A strong Th1 response holds the bacilli tightly in a few granulomas (tuberculoid). A weak Th2 response lets bacilli spread loosely through skin and nerves (lepromatous).

tricks.label: Read the host first
tricks.text: Neonate, older adult, AIDS patient, diabetic in ketoacidosis, or patient on natalizumab: each host narrows the organism list before you read the rest of the stem.

highYield: Neonatal meningitis: group B streptococcus, E. coli, Listeria.
Bacterial CSF: neutrophils, low glucose, high protein.
HSV-1 encephalitis targets the temporal lobes and is hemorrhagic.
Infant botulism comes from spores (honey); adult foodborne botulism comes from preformed toxin.
Tetanus toxin blocks GABA and glycine release from inhibitory interneurons.
PML: JC virus kills oligodendrocytes in AIDS or on natalizumab.
Prions cause spongiform change without inflammation.
Argyll Robertson pupils accommodate but do not react to light (tabes dorsalis).
pitfalls: Eating Taenia solium cysts in undercooked pork gives an intestinal tapeworm; eating eggs from a human carrier gives neurocysticercosis.
Polio and Guillain-Barré both cause flaccid weakness; polio is asymmetric with CSF lymphocytes, while Guillain-Barré is symmetric and ascending with high CSF protein and few cells.
Botulism descends and starts with cranial nerves; Guillain-Barré usually ascends from the legs and causes sensory symptoms.
Toxoplasmosis and CNS lymphoma both ring-enhance in AIDS; PML lesions are white matter lesions that usually do not enhance.
Prion disease and SSPE both cause dementia with myoclonus; SSPE follows childhood measles and has high CSF measles antibody.

summary: Trauma to the brain and spinal cord is tested as a sequence: what the force did, what bled or tore, and how swelling or herniation leads to new signs. Know concussion versus contusion versus diffuse axonal injury, the epidural and subdural hematoma pictures, uncal herniation, and the phases and levels of spinal cord injury.

points: Concussion: trauma-induced, transient loss of normal brain function (confusion, amnesia, sometimes brief loss of consciousness) with normal imaging.
Postconcussion syndrome: headache, dizziness, poor concentration, irritability, and sleep problems that last weeks to months.
Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (dementia pugilistica) follows repeated head injury: memory loss, mood and behavior change, parkinsonism.
CTE pathology: brain atrophy and tau deposits around vessels at the depths of cortical sulci.
notes.why: Concussion is a functional injury: acceleration stretches neuronal membranes and axons, causing ion flux and a surge of glutamate release, followed by a period of high energy demand with reduced cerebral blood flow. This temporary metabolic mismatch explains the symptoms and the normal CT, and it is why a second impact during recovery can cause more damage. With repeated injuries, hyperphosphorylated tau aggregates in neurons and astrocytes around small vessels at the depths of sulci, and the disease can keep progressing years after the head trauma stops.

points: Contusion is a bruise of brain tissue: hemorrhage and necrosis at the crests of gyri.
Coup injury is at the site of impact; contrecoup injury is on the opposite side as the brain rebounds.
The frontal and temporal poles are bruised most because they strike the rough skull base.
Diffuse axonal injury comes from rotational acceleration-deceleration that shears axons, especially in the corpus callosum and brainstem.
Axonal swellings form within hours; the patient is in a coma even though CT shows no mass lesion.
notes.why: Contusions form where the moving brain meets bone: tissue under the impact site is bruised (coup), and the brain is also bruised on the opposite side as it moves within the skull (contrecoup). The orbital frontal and anterior temporal poles are bruised most because they rest on the irregular floors of the anterior and middle cranial fossae. Rotational acceleration creates shear between tissues of different density, and long tracts such as the corpus callosum and brainstem are stretched most. Stretched axons lose axonal transport, so transported material piles up into axonal swellings, and widespread disconnection causes coma with no mass on CT.

points: Epidural hematoma: temporal bone fracture tears the middle meningeal artery; arterial blood strips dura off bone.
Epidural: lens-shaped (biconvex), stopped by suture lines, often a lucid interval then rapid decline.
Subdural hematoma: torn bridging veins between the cortex and dural sinuses; crescent-shaped and crosses suture lines.
Subdural risk: brain atrophy in older adults and people with alcohol use disorder, anticoagulants, and shaken infants.
Chronic subdural hematoma develops over weeks with fluctuating confusion and can rebleed.
Trauma can also cause subarachnoid and intraparenchymal hemorrhage.
notes.why: The vessel that tears sets the location and pace of the bleed. The middle meningeal artery runs between the dura and the thin skull at the pterion, so a fracture there releases arterial blood that peels the dura from bone, and tight dural attachment at the sutures limits spread and gives the lens shape. Bridging veins cross the subdural space, so brain atrophy, which stretches them, lets minor trauma tear them in older adults and people with alcohol use disorder, and violent shaking tears them in infants. Venous blood spreads slowly along the brain surface, giving a crescent that can evolve over weeks.

points: The skull is a fixed box, so an expanding hematoma plus edema raises intracranial pressure and lowers cerebral perfusion pressure (MAP minus ICP).
Uncal herniation: the medial temporal lobe slides under the tentorium and compresses the ipsilateral CN III (dilated, fixed pupil, then down and out).
It also compresses the ipsilateral cerebral peduncle, giving contralateral hemiparesis.
Downward brainstem shift tears small pontine and midbrain branches of the basilar artery: Duret hemorrhages, usually fatal.
Cushing reflex (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing) is a late sign; tonsillar herniation compresses the medulla and stops breathing.
notes.why: Brain, blood, and CSF share a fixed volume inside the skull (Monro-Kellie doctrine), so once CSF and venous blood are pushed out, a small added volume raises pressure steeply. Because cerebral perfusion pressure equals mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure, rising ICP reduces brain blood flow, and brainstem ischemia triggers a sympathetic surge that raises blood pressure while baroreceptors slow the heart (Cushing reflex). Parasympathetic pupillary fibers run on the outer surface of CN III, so the herniating uncus compresses them first and the pupil dilates before the eye turns down and out.

points: Spinal shock comes first: flaccid paralysis, areflexia, sensory loss below the level, and urinary retention.
Neurogenic shock (hypotension with bradycardia) follows high injury because sympathetic outflow (T1 to L2) loses its brain input.
Over days to weeks, reflexes return as upper motor neuron signs: spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign.
The phrenic nerve comes from C3 to C5, so complete injury at or above C3 leaves a ventilator-dependent quadriplegic patient.
Cervical injury below C5 gives quadriplegia with spontaneous breathing; thoracic injury gives paraplegia.
Cord compression (metastasis, epidural abscess, disc): back pain, a sensory level, and upper motor neuron signs.
Cauda equina syndrome (below the cord, which ends about L1 to L2): saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, lost anal reflex, and lower motor neuron leg weakness.
notes.why: Spinal shock reflects the sudden loss of descending facilitation: motor neurons below the lesion lose tonic input from the brain and become hypoexcitable, so reflexes vanish. Over days to weeks the segments below the injury reorganize, and reflexes return exaggerated because descending inhibition is permanently lost, giving the upper motor neuron picture. Injury in the cervical or high thoracic cord (above about T6) cuts brain control of most sympathetic outflow while vagal tone remains, which explains hypotension with bradycardia. Because the cord ends at about L1 to L2, a lesion below that level injures nerve roots and gives lower motor neuron signs.

flows.title: Epidural hematoma
steps: A blow to the side of the head fractures the skull at the pterion.
The fracture tears the middle meningeal artery.
Arterial blood strips dura from bone, forming a biconvex clot.
A lucid interval often follows while the clot keeps expanding.
Mass effect raises intracranial pressure and pushes the uncus under the tentorium.
CN III compression gives an ipsilateral fixed, dilated pupil, then coma.

flows.title: Uncal herniation from an expanding mass
steps: An expanding supratentorial mass adds volume inside the fixed skull.
CSF and venous blood are displaced until compensation runs out.
ICP rises steeply and cerebral perfusion pressure (MAP minus ICP) falls.
The medial temporal uncus herniates under the tentorium.
It compresses ipsilateral CN III and cerebral peduncle: blown pupil, contralateral hemiparesis.
Downward brainstem shift tears basilar artery branches (Duret hemorrhages).

flows.title: Complete spinal cord transection over time
steps: The cord is completely severed at one level.
Spinal shock: flaccid paralysis, areflexia, sensory loss, urinary retention below the level.
Over days to weeks, spinal reflexes return below the level.
Upper motor neuron signs emerge: spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign.

charts.title: Traumatic brain injury types
rows: Temporary functional disturbance, no structural lesion
Confusion or amnesia that resolves; possible postconcussion syndrome
Small vessels and tissue at gyral crests (coup and contrecoup)
Hemorrhagic foci in frontal and temporal poles
Often normal or small hemorrhages in corpus callosum and brainstem
Immediate coma without a mass lesion
Middle meningeal artery after temporal bone fracture
Gradual or fluctuating decline; acute or chronic
Neurons with tau deposits after repeated injury

charts.title: Spinal cord compression versus cauda equina syndrome
rows: Above the conus (cord ends about L1 to L2)
Lumbar and sacral nerve roots below the cord
Upper motor neuron: spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski (after spinal shock)
Lower motor neuron: flaccid, often asymmetric leg weakness, reduced reflexes
Urinary retention early, lost anal reflex and sphincter tone
Vertebral metastasis (lung, breast, prostate), epidural abscess, trauma
Large central disc herniation, tumor, epidural abscess

tricks.label: Epidural is arterial and fast
tricks.text: Epidural blood is arterial (middle meningeal), so it expands fast after a lucid interval. Subdural blood is venous (bridging veins), so it often builds slowly, especially in an atrophic brain.

tricks.label: C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive
tricks.text: The phrenic nerve comes from C3, C4, and C5. A complete cord injury at or above C3 stops diaphragm breathing.

tricks.label: Blown pupil side
tricks.text: In uncal herniation the dilated pupil is on the same side as the mass, and the weakness is on the opposite side from the compressed peduncle.

highYield: Concussion has normal imaging; diffuse axonal injury causes coma with little on CT.
Contusions favor the frontal and temporal poles.
Epidural hematoma: middle meningeal artery, temporal bone fracture, lucid interval, biconvex.
Subdural hematoma: bridging veins, crescent shape, older adults and shaken infants.
Uncal herniation: ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil, contralateral hemiparesis, then Duret hemorrhages.
Spinal shock gives flaccid areflexia first; spasticity and hyperreflexia come later.
Cauda equina syndrome: saddle anesthesia and urinary retention.
pitfalls: A lucid interval is classic for epidural hematoma but is not always present, and it can occur with subdural hematoma.
Spinal shock looks like a lower motor neuron lesion at first; the upper motor neuron picture appears only as reflexes return.
Neurogenic shock (bradycardia, warm skin) differs from hemorrhagic shock (tachycardia, cold skin).
Kernohan notch: compression of the opposite cerebral peduncle against the tentorium can cause weakness on the same side as the mass, a false localizing sign.

dumps.p: Draw a coronal section of the brain with a temporal epidural hematoma. Use arrows to trace how it leads to herniation and death, and label each sign along the way.
l: Temporal bone fracture tears the middle meningeal artery
Biconvex arterial clot between dura and skull
Rising intracranial pressure and falling perfusion pressure
Uncus herniates under the tentorium
Ipsilateral CN III compression: fixed dilated pupil
Ipsilateral cerebral peduncle compression: contralateral hemiparesis
Brainstem shifts down and Duret hemorrhages form
Cushing reflex and respiratory arrest

dumps.p: Draw the spinal cord from C1 to the cauda equina. Mark C3 to C5, the sympathetic outflow, and where the cord ends, then write what a complete injury at C2, C6, T10, and below L2 would cause.
l: C2: quadriplegia and ventilator dependence (above phrenic roots)
C6: quadriplegia with diaphragm breathing
T10: paraplegia
Below L2: cauda equina syndrome with lower motor neuron signs
Sympathetic outflow T1 to L2; high injury causes neurogenic shock
Spinal shock first, then spasticity and hyperreflexia
Cord ends about L1 to L2

summary: Peripheral nerve and root problems are anatomy questions in disguise. Each one asks which nerve or root is pinched, where it runs, and what it supplies, so the exam can predict the exact numb area, weak muscle, and lost reflex. Learn the cranial nerve palsies, the wrist and elbow tunnels, and the cervical and lumbar root levels.

points: Bell palsy: idiopathic lower motor neuron CN VII palsy, linked to HSV reactivation, diabetes, pregnancy, and Lyme disease.
Bell palsy weakens the whole half of the face, forehead included; a stroke (upper motor neuron) spares the forehead because the upper face has input from both hemispheres.
Branches inside the facial canal explain the extras: less tearing (greater petrosal), hyperacusis (stapedius), lost taste on the front two-thirds of the tongue (chorda tympani).
Trigeminal neuralgia: seconds-long electric-shock pain in V2 or V3, triggered by touch, chewing, or brushing teeth.
Usual cause is a blood vessel loop pressing on the trigeminal root; in a young patient, think of a multiple sclerosis plaque.
notes.why: Bell palsy is thought to result from inflammation of CN VII, likely from HSV reactivation, which swells the nerve inside the narrow bony facial canal. A lesion of the nerve itself weakens the whole half of the face, and its level along the canal decides which branches also fail (tearing, stapedius, taste). A stroke spares the forehead because the part of the facial nucleus that supplies the forehead receives input from both motor cortices. In trigeminal neuralgia, vessel pulsation or an MS plaque demyelinates the root, and the bare axons fire abnormally, so light touch triggers bursts of pain.

points: Carpal tunnel syndrome: median nerve squeezed under the flexor retinaculum.
Risks: pregnancy, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, acromegaly, dialysis-related amyloid, repetitive wrist use.
Findings: night paresthesia of the thumb, index, middle, and half the ring finger; thenar atrophy; positive Tinel and Phalen signs.
Palm sensation is spared because the palmar cutaneous branch leaves before the tunnel and runs over the retinaculum.
Cubital tunnel: ulnar nerve at the medial epicondyle; numb ring and little fingers, weak intrinsic hand muscles.
Thoracic outlet syndrome: cervical rib or scalene muscles compress the lower trunk (C8 to T1), subclavian artery, or vein.
TOS gives ulnar-side hand paresthesia and intrinsic hand weakness, with arm pallor, coolness, or swelling when the vessels are involved, often worse with the arm overhead.
notes.why: Entrapment injures a nerve inside a tight, fixed space: pressure first reduces blood flow in the small vessels of the nerve and causes focal demyelination, and longer or heavier compression damages axons. Anything that adds volume to the carpal tunnel, such as fluid in pregnancy, glycosaminoglycan deposits in hypothyroidism, synovitis in rheumatoid arthritis, or amyloid in dialysis patients, compresses the median nerve because the flexor retinaculum cannot stretch. Symptoms worsen at night because the wrist often flexes during sleep, which raises tunnel pressure. In thoracic outlet syndrome the lower trunk sits lowest in the plexus, so a cervical rib or fibrous band presses on C8 and T1, giving ulnar-side symptoms.

points: Disc herniation: the nucleus pulposus pushes through a torn annulus fibrosus, usually posterolaterally at L4 to L5 or L5 to S1.
A posterolateral lumbar herniation hits the lower root: an L4 to L5 disc compresses L5, and an L5 to S1 disc compresses S1.
Cervical roots exit above their vertebra, so a C5 to C6 disc compresses C6 and a C6 to C7 disc compresses C7.
Radiculopathy (root entrapment by disc, osteophytes, or foraminal narrowing) gives dermatomal pain, myotomal weakness, and a lost reflex.
Sciatica: pain from the buttock down the back of the thigh and below the knee, usually from L5 or S1; a straight leg raise reproduces it.
notes.why: The posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow and does not cover the posterolateral annulus, so the nucleus pulposus usually herniates there. In the lumbar spine each root exits below its own pedicle, and the root crossing the disc to exit one level lower is the one compressed, so an L4 to L5 disc hits L5. Cervical roots exit above their vertebrae, so a C5 to C6 disc hits C6. Compression plus inflammatory chemicals released from the nucleus irritate the root, producing dermatomal pain, weakness of its muscles, and a reduced reflex, and a straight leg raise stretches the L5 and S1 roots to reproduce sciatica.

points: Common fibular nerve at the fibular neck (fracture, leg crossing, tight cast): foot drop, weak eversion, numb lateral leg and dorsum of foot.
Inversion is spared in fibular nerve palsy (tibialis posterior is tibial) but weak in L5 radiculopathy, which tells them apart.
Tarsal tunnel syndrome: tibial nerve behind the medial malleolus; burning and numbness of the sole.
notes.why: The common fibular nerve wraps around the fibular neck just under the skin, so it is easily compressed against bone by leg crossing, a cast, or a fracture. Its deep branch supplies the dorsiflexors and its superficial branch supplies the evertors and lateral leg skin, so injury causes foot drop, weak eversion, and lateral leg numbness. The L5 root also reaches tibialis posterior through the tibial nerve, so weak inversion places the lesion at the root. In the tarsal tunnel, the tibial nerve passes under the flexor retinaculum behind the medial malleolus, so compression there numbs the sole through the plantar nerves.

points: Lumbar spinal stenosis: neurogenic claudication, with leg pain on standing and walking that eases with sitting or bending forward; pulses are normal.
Cervical stenosis compresses the cord: myelopathy with clumsy hands, unsteady gait, and upper motor neuron signs in the legs.
Complex regional pain syndrome: burning pain out of proportion, allodynia, swelling, and skin color, temperature, and sweating changes after a limb injury.
CRPS type I has no identifiable nerve injury; type II follows a nerve injury.
Phantom limb pain is pain felt in an amputated limb, linked to cortical remapping and nerve-end neuromas.
notes.why: In lumbar stenosis, disc bulging, facet hypertrophy, and a thickened ligamentum flavum narrow the canal, and standing extends the spine and narrows it further while walking raises the metabolic demand of the crowded roots. Flexion widens the canal, which is why sitting or leaning forward relieves symptoms, and normal pulses separate this from vascular claudication. Cervical stenosis compresses the cord itself, so it produces upper motor neuron signs below the level. CRPS combines exaggerated local inflammation, sensitized peripheral and central pain pathways, and disturbed autonomic control after an injury, which explains pain out of proportion along with swelling and changes in skin color, temperature, and sweating.

flows.title: Facial nerve path and the branches it loses
steps: CN VII leaves the pons and enters the internal acoustic meatus.
At the geniculate ganglion, the greater petrosal nerve leaves for the lacrimal gland.
In the facial canal, the nerve to stapedius leaves to damp loud sound.
The chorda tympani leaves next, carrying taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
The nerve exits the stylomastoid foramen to supply the muscles of facial expression.

flows.title: Carpal tunnel syndrome
steps: Added volume (fluid, synovitis, deposits) fills the rigid carpal tunnel.
Pressure rises on the median nerve under the flexor retinaculum.
Reduced blood flow in the nerve's small vessels causes focal demyelination.
Night paresthesia in the thumb, index, middle, and half the ring finger.
Sustained compression causes axonal loss with thenar weakness and atrophy.

flows.title: Lumbar disc herniation to S1 sciatica
steps: Degeneration and load tear the posterolateral annulus fibrosus.
The nucleus pulposus herniates posterolaterally at L5 to S1.
The herniation compresses and inflames the traversing S1 root.
Pain radiates from the buttock down the back of the leg (sciatica).
S1 deficits: weak plantarflexion, lateral foot numbness, lost ankle reflex.

charts.title: Root lesions
rows: Elbow extension (triceps), wrist flexion, finger extension
Lateral leg, dorsum of foot, big toe
Big toe extension, ankle dorsiflexion and inversion, hip abduction

charts.title: Peripheral compression syndromes
rows: CN VII in the facial canal
HSV reactivation, diabetes, pregnancy, Lyme disease
Whole half-face weakness, hyperacusis, lost anterior taste, dry eye
Pregnancy, hypothyroidism, RA, diabetes, dialysis amyloid
Night paresthesia of lateral 3.5 fingers, thenar atrophy, palm spared
Lower root compressed (L4 to L5 disc hits L5)
Pain below the knee, positive straight leg raise
Lower trunk C8 to T1, subclavian artery or vein
Ulnar-side paresthesia, intrinsic weakness, arm pallor or swelling
Vascular loop; MS in young patients
Brief lancinating V2 or V3 pain with trigger zones
Fourth and fifth finger paresthesia, weak interossei
Common fibular nerve at fibular neck
Fibular neck fracture, leg crossing, cast
Foot drop, weak eversion, numb dorsum of foot

tricks.label: Forehead test
tricks.text: Can the patient wrinkle the forehead? If yes, the lesion is upper motor neuron (stroke). If no, the facial nerve itself is damaged (Bell palsy).

tricks.label: Lumbar disc hits the next root down
tricks.text: Name the lower vertebra in the disc level and that is the root hit by a typical posterolateral herniation: L4 to L5 gives L5, L5 to S1 gives S1.

tricks.label: S1, S2 buckle my shoe; L3, L4 kick the door; C5, C6 pick up sticks; C7, C8 lay them straight
tricks.text: Reflex levels: Achilles S1 to S2, patellar L3 to L4, biceps C5 to C6, triceps C7 to C8.

highYield: Bell palsy paralyzes the forehead; a stroke spares it.
Carpal tunnel spares palm sensation because the palmar cutaneous branch runs above the retinaculum.
An L5 to S1 disc herniation compresses S1: lost Achilles reflex, weak plantar flexion.
L5 root lesion: weak big toe extension and foot dorsiflexion, numb dorsum of foot.
Thoracic outlet syndrome affects C8 to T1, so symptoms are on the ulnar side of the hand.
Trigeminal neuralgia in a young adult suggests multiple sclerosis.
Neurogenic claudication eases with bending forward; vascular claudication eases with stopping, regardless of posture.
pitfalls: Foot drop from common fibular palsy spares inversion; foot drop from L5 radiculopathy weakens inversion.
Carpal tunnel numbness spares the palm; a more proximal median nerve lesion numbs the palm too.
Cubital tunnel syndrome numbs the dorsal ulnar hand; ulnar compression at the wrist (Guyon canal) spares it because the dorsal branch leaves above the wrist.
Cervical stenosis produces upper motor neuron signs in the legs; lumbar stenosis produces only root symptoms.
Thoracic outlet syndrome and cubital tunnel syndrome both numb the ulnar fingers; TOS also numbs the medial forearm and can add arm pallor or swelling.

dumps.p: Draw the outline of an arm and a leg. Shade the dermatomes for C6, C7, L4, L5, and S1, and next to each write the weak muscle and the reflex that is lost.
l: C6: thumb and lateral forearm; elbow flexion and wrist extension; biceps and brachioradialis reflexes
C7: middle finger; triceps; triceps reflex
L4: medial leg; quadriceps; patellar reflex
L5: dorsum of foot and big toe; big toe extension and dorsiflexion; no reliable reflex
S1: lateral foot and sole; plantar flexion; Achilles reflex
Lumbar posterolateral disc hits the lower root
Cervical C5 to C6 disc hits C6

dumps.p: Trace the facial nerve from the pons through the facial canal to the face. Label each branch and write what a patient loses with Bell palsy and why a stroke looks different.
l: Greater petrosal nerve: lacrimal gland, reduced tearing
Nerve to stapedius: hyperacusis
Chorda tympani: taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue
Motor branches: whole half-face weakness including the forehead
Corneal exposure because the eye cannot close
Upper motor neuron lesion spares the forehead (bilateral cortical input)
Associations: HSV, diabetes, pregnancy, Lyme disease

summary: Eye and ear diseases are tested by matching the symptom pattern (pain or no pain, sudden or gradual, central or peripheral vision, hearing loss or not) to the structure that failed. Learn the red eye differential, the causes of vision loss, the retinal findings of systemic disease, and the vertigo and hearing loss patterns.

points: Blepharitis: anterior from staphylococcal or seborrheic disease at the lash base; posterior from meibomian gland dysfunction.
Hordeolum (stye) is an acute, painful gland infection, usually S. aureus; a chalazion is a painless meibomian lipogranuloma.
Keratitis: HSV gives a branching dendritic ulcer; contact lens wearers get Pseudomonas or Acanthamoeba ulcers.
Pterygium is a UV-related fibrovascular growth of conjunctiva onto the cornea, usually on the nasal side.
Corneal abrasion and corneal foreign body take up fluorescein; subconjunctival hemorrhage is a painless red patch with normal vision.
Alkali burns cause liquefactive necrosis and penetrate deeper than acid burns, which cause coagulative necrosis.
notes.why: The cornea is avascular and densely innervated by V1, so corneal injury is painful, and any break in the epithelium lets fluorescein stain the exposed area. HSV reactivates from the trigeminal ganglion and spreads from cell to cell along the corneal epithelium, producing a branching dendritic ulcer. Contact lenses cause epithelial microtrauma and hypoxia and can carry organisms from contaminated water or solution, which explains Pseudomonas and Acanthamoeba keratitis. Alkali saponifies membrane lipids and keeps penetrating as liquefactive necrosis, while acid coagulates surface proteins into a barrier that limits its own spread.

points: Cataract is opacified lens protein: painless gradual blur, glare, loss of the red reflex.
Cataract risks: age, diabetes (sorbitol), galactosemia (galactitol), corticosteroids, UV light, smoking, congenital rubella.
Glaucoma is an optic neuropathy with cupping of the optic disc and visual field loss.
Open-angle glaucoma: poor outflow through the trabecular meshwork, painless loss of peripheral vision.
Acute angle-closure glaucoma: the iris blocks the angle; painful red eye, halos, nausea, a fixed mid-dilated pupil. Pupil dilation can trigger it.
Anterior uveitis (iritis): ciliary flush, photophobia, small irregular pupil; linked to HLA-B27 disease, sarcoidosis, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
Posterior uveitis and chorioretinitis: toxoplasmosis, and CMV retinitis in AIDS.
Lens dislocation: upward in Marfan syndrome, downward in homocystinuria.
notes.why: Lens clarity depends on tightly ordered crystallin proteins; in diabetes and galactosemia, aldose reductase turns glucose or galactose into sorbitol or galactitol, which is trapped in the lens, draws in water, and clouds it. Aqueous humor drains through the trabecular meshwork into the canal of Schlemm, and raised intraocular pressure from poor outflow, the main modifiable risk factor, damages ganglion cell axons at the optic disc. In a shallow anterior chamber, a mid-dilated pupil lets the peripheral iris bunch into the angle, which is why dilation can trigger angle closure. Lens dislocation reflects weak zonular fibers, from defective fibrillin in Marfan syndrome or abnormal zonules in homocystinuria.

points: Dry macular degeneration: drusen and slow central vision loss. Wet: VEGF-driven choroidal neovessels that leak and bleed, causing rapid central loss and distortion.
Age and smoking are the main risks for macular degeneration.
Central retinal artery occlusion: sudden painless monocular loss, pale retina, cherry-red spot. Amaurosis fugax is a brief version from carotid emboli.
Central retinal vein occlusion: diffuse retinal hemorrhages and swollen, tortuous veins.
Retinal detachment: flashes, floaters, then a curtain over the vision; myopia raises the risk.
Retinitis pigmentosa: inherited photoreceptor loss with night blindness, tunnel vision, and bone spicule pigment.
notes.why: The outer retina depends on the retinal pigment epithelium and choroid; with age, drusen build up beneath the RPE, and the RPE and photoreceptors slowly die (dry disease). In wet disease, VEGF signaling drives choroidal vessels through Bruch membrane, and their leakage and bleeding cause rapid central loss, which is why anti-VEGF injections are used. The central retinal artery is an end artery to the inner retina, so occlusion turns the retina pale, while the fovea, which lacks inner retinal layers and is fed by the choroid, stays red (cherry-red spot). Long myopic eyes have a stretched, thinner retina that tears more easily.

points: Acute otitis media: eustachian tube dysfunction in children lets middle ear fluid get infected (S. pneumoniae, nontypeable H. influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis).
Otitis media complications: perforation, mastoiditis, cholesteatoma, and conductive hearing loss; otitis media with effusion is fluid without acute infection.
Otitis externa: Pseudomonas or S. aureus, pain on pulling the pinna or pressing the tragus.
Malignant otitis externa: Pseudomonas skull base osteomyelitis in older diabetics, with cranial nerve palsies (often CN VII).
Auricular perichondritis: infection of the ear cartilage, often Pseudomonas, after a high (cartilage) ear piercing; red, painful, swollen pinna that spares the lobule.
Ménière disease: endolymphatic hydrops with vertigo lasting hours, fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural loss, tinnitus, and ear fullness.
Vestibular neuritis: continuous vertigo for days with normal hearing; labyrinthitis adds hearing loss.
BPPV: loose otoconia in the posterior canal give brief vertigo with head movement and a positive Dix-Hallpike test.
notes.why: In young children the eustachian tube is shorter and more horizontal, so it drains poorly and lets nasopharyngeal bacteria reach the middle ear after a viral infection swells the tube. Pseudomonas thrives in moist, damaged skin and poorly perfused cartilage, and in older diabetics it can invade the skull base near the stylomastoid foramen, where CN VII exits. Ménière disease is excess endolymph distending the membranous labyrinth, which disturbs both the cochlea and the vestibular organs. In BPPV, loose otoconia in the posterior canal move with gravity when the head turns, deflecting the cupula and causing brief vertigo with nystagmus.

points: Myopia focuses in front of the retina (long eye); hyperopia behind it (short eye); astigmatism comes from uneven corneal curvature.
Presbyopia is age-related loss of lens elasticity that makes near vision hard.
Childhood strabismus causes amblyopia because the brain suppresses the deviating eye's input.
Conductive hearing loss blocks sound before the cochlea; sensorineural loss damages hair cells or CN VIII. Both can cause tinnitus.
notes.why: An eye that is too long focuses light in front of the retina (myopia), and one that is too short focuses behind it (hyperopia). For near vision the ciliary muscle contracts, which relaxes the zonules and lets the elastic lens round up; as the lens stiffens with age, this accommodation fails (presbyopia). In early childhood the visual cortex keeps connections that receive matched input from both eyes, so a deviating eye loses its cortical connections and vision stays poor unless treated early. Conductive loss blocks the air path through the ear canal and ossicles, while sensorineural loss damages the cochlea or CN VIII.

flows.title: Aqueous humor flow and open-angle glaucoma
steps: Ciliary body epithelium secretes aqueous humor into the posterior chamber.
Aqueous passes through the pupil into the anterior chamber.
It drains through the trabecular meshwork into the canal of Schlemm.
Poor outflow through the meshwork raises intraocular pressure.
Pressure damages ganglion cell axons at the optic disc, enlarging the cup.
Peripheral visual field loss develops painlessly.

flows.title: Acute angle-closure glaucoma
steps: A shallow anterior chamber (hyperopia, older age, large lens) narrows the angle.
Mid-dilation of the pupil increases iris contact with the lens (pupillary block).
Aqueous builds up behind the iris and bows it forward.
The peripheral iris seals off the trabecular meshwork.
Pressure rises sharply: painful red eye, halos, nausea, fixed mid-dilated pupil.

flows.title: Acute otitis media in a child
steps: A viral upper respiratory infection swells the eustachian tube.
The middle ear cannot ventilate, and fluid collects behind the eardrum.
Nasopharyngeal bacteria reach the trapped fluid through the tube.
Infection causes a bulging red tympanic membrane, ear pain, and fever.
Pressure can perforate the eardrum or spread infection to the mastoid.

charts.title: Eye conditions
rows: Age, diabetes, galactosemia, steroids, UV, smoking, congenital rubella
Lens protein opacification; sorbitol or galactitol draw water into the lens
Painless blur, glare, lost red reflex
Red eye with discharge, normal vision
Open-angle: age, family history; angle-closure: narrow angle, pupil dilation
Optic nerve damage, often from high intraocular pressure
Disc cupping and field loss; acute closure is painful with a mid-dilated pupil
Ciliary flush, photophobia; dendritic or corneal ulcer
Central vision loss, distortion in wet form
Anterior: HLA-B27, sarcoidosis, JIA; posterior: toxoplasmosis, CMV
Inflammation of iris, ciliary body, or choroid
Pain and photophobia (anterior); floaters and blurred vision (posterior)

charts.title: Conjunctivitis types
rows: Watery, preauricular lymph node, very contagious
S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae
Purulent, lids stuck together in the morning
Copious pus, rapid onset, risk of corneal perforation
C. trachomatis (serotypes D to K inclusion conjunctivitis; A to C trachoma)
Chronic follicular conjunctivitis; trachoma scars the lid and cornea and causes blindness

charts.title: Retinal findings
rows: Arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking, flame hemorrhages, cotton wool spots
Microaneurysms, dot-blot hemorrhages, hard exudates; neovascularization when proliferative
Gradual loss; vitreous hemorrhage or detachment when proliferative
Bilateral swollen discs with blurred margins
Headache from raised intracranial pressure, vision usually normal early

charts.title: Ear conditions and vertigo
rows: S. pneumoniae, nontypeable H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis
Mild conductive loss from canal swelling
Conductive loss from canal swelling; deep pain and cranial nerve palsies
Fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural loss, tinnitus, fullness
Inflamed vestibular nerve, often after a viral illness
Otoconia in the posterior semicircular canal

charts.title: Hearing loss and other eye problems
rows: Cerumen, perforation, barotrauma, eustachian tube dysfunction, otosclerosis (stapes fixation), cholesteatoma
Weber lateralizes to the bad ear; bone conduction beats air conduction
Presbycusis (high frequencies), noise-induced hair cell damage
Weber lateralizes to the good ear; air conduction beats bone conduction
Preseptal cellulitis versus orbital cellulitis (often from ethmoid sinusitis)
Pain with eye movement, proptosis, and ophthalmoplegia mean orbital
Dacryocystitis (blocked nasolacrimal duct); endophthalmitis (after surgery or trauma)
Hyphema (blood in the anterior chamber); orbital floor fracture
Floor fracture traps inferior rectus and limits upward gaze

tricks.label: Pupil in a painful red eye
tricks.text: Small and irregular means iritis. Fixed and mid-dilated means acute angle closure. A normal pupil with discharge points to conjunctivitis.

tricks.label: Time the vertigo
tricks.text: Seconds with head movement is BPPV. Hours with hearing changes is Ménière disease. Days of constant vertigo is vestibular neuritis, or labyrinthitis if hearing is also lost.

tricks.label: Sugar alcohols cloud the lens
tricks.text: Aldose reductase turns glucose into sorbitol and galactose into galactitol. These pull water into the lens, so diabetes and galactosemia both cause cataracts.

highYield: Acute angle-closure glaucoma: painful red eye, halos, fixed mid-dilated pupil; dilation triggers it.
Wet macular degeneration is VEGF-driven choroidal neovascularization.
Cherry-red spot plus sudden painless monocular loss means central retinal artery occlusion.
Anterior uveitis links to HLA-B27, sarcoidosis, and JIA.
HSV keratitis gives a dendritic ulcer on fluorescein.
Ménière disease: episodic vertigo, low-frequency hearing loss, tinnitus, fullness.
Malignant otitis externa: Pseudomonas, older diabetic, cranial nerve palsies.
Orbital floor fracture traps the inferior rectus and limits upward gaze.
pitfalls: Hordeolum hurts and is infected; chalazion is painless and granulomatous.
Vestibular neuritis and labyrinthitis feel the same, but only labyrinthitis causes hearing loss.
Preseptal cellulitis can look dramatic, but eye movement and vision stay normal; orbital cellulitis limits eye movement.
Open-angle glaucoma is painless and steals peripheral vision first; macular degeneration steals central vision first.
Marfan lens goes up, homocystinuria lens goes down.

dumps.p: Build a table with rows for viral, bacterial, gonococcal, and allergic conjunctivitis, keratitis, anterior uveitis, and acute angle-closure glaucoma. Columns: pain, vision, pupil, discharge, key clue.
l: Viral: watery, preauricular node, normal vision
Bacterial: purulent; gonococcal is hyperacute with heavy pus
Allergic: itching, both eyes
Keratitis: pain, fluorescein uptake, dendrite in HSV, contact lens link
Anterior uveitis: ciliary flush, photophobia, small irregular pupil
Angle closure: severe pain, halos, nausea, fixed mid-dilated pupil
Vision is normal in conjunctivitis and reduced in the others

dumps.p: Draw the outer, middle, and inner ear. Label where otitis externa, otitis media, otosclerosis, cholesteatoma, Ménière disease, BPPV, and vestibular neuritis occur, and mark each as conductive or sensorineural if it causes hearing loss.
l: Outer canal: otitis externa (Pseudomonas, tragal pain)
Middle ear: otitis media from eustachian tube dysfunction; conductive loss
Stapes footplate fixed at the oval window in otosclerosis; conductive
Cholesteatoma erodes ossicles; conductive
Cochlea and endolymph: Ménière disease; sensorineural
Posterior semicircular canal: BPPV otoconia
Vestibular nerve: vestibular neuritis with normal hearing
Weber and Rinne patterns for each type of loss
